title: Publication and companion poem
short: First published in 1845 as part I of 'Night and Morning'; in 1849 Browning separated it, with 'Parting at Morning' as its pendant.
body: The archive's collection label (Dramatic Lyrics, 1842) is not right for this poem. It first appeared in Dramatic Romances and Lyrics (1845) as the first part of a two-part poem, 'Night and Morning'. In Poems (1849) Browning separated the parts as 'Meeting at Night' and 'Parting at Morning'. The four-line sequel has the lover leave at dawn for 'the need of a world of men'. The pronouns of the sequel make the traveller a man. This matters for interpretation. Read alone, 'Meeting at Night' ends in rapture; read with its pair, the rapture is a single episode in a larger life of work. Some modern critics call it the most sensual poem Browning had written up to that date and link it to his feelings for Elizabeth Barrett.

title: Form: two sestets without a main verb
short: Two six-line stanzas rhymed abccba (envelope rhyme), in loose four-stress lines. The whole poem is a sequence of noun phrases with no main clause.
body: Each stanza rhymes abccba (land / low / leap / sleep / prow / sand; beach / appears / scratch / match / fears / each), so the stanza closes in on itself as the journey closes in on the meeting. The lines have four stresses with a mix of iambs and anapaests, which gives a rocking, propulsive movement. Grammatically the poem has no finite main verb. It is a list of sensations joined by 'And' and 'Then', with verbs only in subordinate clauses ('As I gain the cove'). The syntax imitates perception in a hurry, impressions arriving one after another before any reflection. The meeting itself is reached only in the last line.

title: Gray, black, yellow
short: The opening paints a night seascape in three colours, gray sea, black land and a large low yellow moon, with heavy, slow stresses.
body: Line 1 is heavily stressed ('gray sea', 'long black land'), and so the poem opens slowly and broadly before the quickening of line 3. The palette is sparse. Against it the 'yellow half-moon large and low' (a moon near the horizon looks enlarged) is the first point of warmth. Colour later sharpens into the 'fiery ringlets' of the waves and the 'blue spurt' of the match, so the poem moves from dim expanse to points of light.

sources.cite: John Pettigrew and Thomas J. Collins (eds), Robert Browning: The Poems (Penguin, 1981), vol. 1, notes

anchor: In fiery ringlets from their sleep
title: Fiery ringlets
short: The waves 'startled' by the boat leap up in rings of fire, probably sea phosphorescence stirred by the prow, imagined as sleepers woken.
body: Small waves disturbed by the boat light up as 'fiery ringlets'. The usual explanation is marine phosphorescence (bioluminescent plankton glowing when disturbed), though the moonlight on curling ripples may be meant as well. The waves are personified: 'startled', woken 'from their sleep', they 'leap'. 'Ringlets' are also curls of hair, and the word looks forward to the woman waiting at the end. The nervous excitement of the waves anticipates the 'joys and fears' of line 11.

sources.cite: John Pettigrew and Thomas J. Collins (eds), Robert Browning: The Poems (Penguin, 1981), vol. 1, notes

title: Pushing prow, slushy sand
short: The boat drives into the cove and its speed is 'quench[ed]' in the wet sand. Many readers hear a veiled sexual suggestion in the movement.
body: 'Gain' means reach, arrive at. The boat's 'pushing prow' enters the cove and its speed is quenched 'i' the slushy sand' (the elided 'i'' for 'in' is typical Browning colloquialism). The physical vigour of the lines, with the plosives of 'pushing prow', is plain. Many critics also find an erotic subtext, the journey's thrust and its quenching anticipating the lovers' meeting. Others warn against over-reading and stress the realism of a night landing on a beach. Either way, the first stanza ends with arrival by sea and the second begins the journey on land.

title: Shift of senses
short: In the second stanza sight gives way to smell, touch and sound: warmth, sea scent, a tap, a scratch, a voice.
body: The first stanza is mostly visual. In the second, as the speaker comes nearer, the senses become intimate: warmth and scent ('warm sea-scented beach'), then hearing ('A tap', 'scratch', 'a voice'), then the felt heartbeat. The compound 'sea-scented' keeps the sea with him on land. The distances shrink, from 'a mile' of beach to 'Three fields' to a window pane, a kind of zoom that suits the poem's single forward motion.

sources.cite: John Pettigrew and Thomas J. Collins (eds), Robert Browning: The Poems (Penguin, 1981), vol. 1, notes

title: Tap at the pane
short: The secret signal: a tap at the window, answered from inside by striking a match.
body: The lover does not knock at the door. He taps at the window, which suggests a clandestine meeting and perhaps a prearranged signal. The farmhouse ('till a farm appears') places the woman in a rural, domestic setting. The response is immediate, a match struck inside, so the reader learns she has been waiting. The lines give no names and no explanation, which is typical of Browning's dramatic lyric. The situation is caught in the middle of the action.

title: Scratch and blue spurt of a match
short: The friction match, still a fairly recent invention in 1845, gives the poem's most precisely observed and sounded image.
body: 'Quick sharp scratch / And blue spurt of a lighted match' is strongly onomatopoeic. The short vowels and clustered consonants (sk, tch) imitate the strike, and 'spurt' catches the flare's sudden burst of blue before it settles. Friction matches had been on sale in England only since the late 1820s, so the detail is pointedly modern. It brings an unpoetic object into a love lyric. The tiny flame is the climax of the poem's movement from darkness towards light.

sources.cite: John Pettigrew and Thomas J. Collins (eds), Robert Browning: The Poems (Penguin, 1981), vol. 1, notes

anchor: two hearts beating each to each
title: Two hearts beating
short: The meeting ends in a whisper quieter than the lovers' heartbeats. Read with 'Parting at Morning', the rapture is only half the story.
body: The final lines compare a 'voice less loud, through its joys and fears' with the 'two hearts beating each to each'. The whispered greeting is fainter than the sound of the lovers' pulses, and the poem ends at the moment of meeting, without describing it. 'Each to each' suggests mutual answering, two rhythms in step. Whose voice it is (hers, or both) is left open. The ending's self-sufficient rapture is qualified by the poem's original pairing. In 'Parting at Morning' the man turns away from love to the world of men. Critics disagree on whether that sequel undercuts the night's experience or completes it.
